opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the relationship is quite deep, and in a sense it's the central puzzle. Language, like images, is not just a bag of correlations. It has a hierarchical, compositional structure: letters form words, words form phrases, phrases form sentences, and at each level the meaning of the whole depends on how the parts are combined. If data had no such structure, learning it in high dimension would be hopeless. You'd face the curse of dimensionality, and the number of examples you'd need would be astronomically large. So the fact that these models work at all tells us they must be exploiting some hidden structure in the data.

What we've tried to do in my group is make this precise with simple generative models of data, like what we call the random hierarchy model, a kind of random context-free grammar. You can generate data from it, train networks on it, and ask: how many examples do you need to learn the structure, and how is that structure represented inside the network? What comes out is quite intuitive once you see it. The network discovers the hierarchy level by level. Low-level structure, like which tokens tend to go together locally, is detected from correlations with relatively few samples. Higher-level structure only becomes visible once you have enough data to resolve correlations at larger scales. So the sample complexity is set by how fast those correlations decay with distance, and how much data you need to build latent "synonym" representations, groups of tokens that play the same role.

That gives a nice picture of scaling laws. As you increase the training set, the model can resolve correlations at larger and larger distances, and it builds deeper levels of the hierarchy. The steady improvement in loss that people observe empirically is then not mysterious. It reflects the progressive acquisition of more abstract structure.

For building better generative models, I think the lesson is twofold. First, if we understand what structure the data has and how it's learned, we can reason about architecture: what inductive biases help a network compose representations hierarchically, and why depth matters. Second, it shapes how we think about generation itself. In diffusion models, for example, we've seen that as you add noise, you first destroy low-level details while high-level features survive, and then at some critical noise level there's something like a phase transition where the high-level class changes. That's exactly what you'd expect if the data is hierarchical. It suggests generation is fundamentally about recombining features at different levels of abstraction, which is also what creativity looks like.

So understanding the hidden hierarchy is more than an academic exercise. It's what tells us why these models generalize, how much data they need, and where we might make them more efficient. Right now we scale mostly by trial and error. A theory of the structure of data could make that much more principled.

r001.rationale: The response confidently says hidden structure explains model learning and generalization; it does not express uncertainty about whether fully understanding that hierarchy can help token-level prediction.

r002.rationale: It discusses learning hierarchical structure and generating by recombining features, but does not distinguish understanding structure as an encoding problem from producing low-level data as a decoding problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think this is really the central question for me, because when we started working on this, the motivation was a very basic puzzle in high-dimensional statistics. If you look at the space of all possible sequences of words, or the space of all possible images, it is enormous. The number of sentences of length a hundred is astronomical. So a naive learner, one that just tries to memorize or interpolate in that space, is hopeless. It would need an amount of data that grows exponentially with the dimension. This is the curse of dimensionality. And yet these models learn with, let's say, a trillion tokens, which is a lot, but it is nothing compared to that exponential. So something about the data must be special, and the question is what.

Our view, and it is of course not only ours, people in linguistics have said this for a very long time, is that the structure is hierarchical and compositional. A sentence is made of phrases, phrases are made of words, words of characters. And the key point is that the low-level objects are, to some extent, interchangeable. You can swap one noun phrase for another and the sentence is still grammatical, it still has the same high-level meaning. So there is a hierarchy of latent variables, and each latent variable at one level is generated from the one above with some noise, some freedom in how it is expressed.

What we did was build a toy version of this, a random hierarchy model, where you have a tree of latent variables, and the rules of the grammar are drawn at random. And the nice thing is that you can then compute how many data points a deep network needs to learn it. And the answer is that it is polynomial in the dimension, not exponential. The reason is that the network does not have to learn the whole thing at once. It can learn the lowest-level rules first, discover that these groups of characters are synonyms because they appear in the same contexts, and then that gives it a representation that is lower dimensional, and it climbs the hierarchy one level at a time.

Now, how does this connect to generative models and language in particular? I think in two ways. The first is that it gives you a prediction about what happens during training, and also as you scale data. You should see the model acquire the structure from the bottom up. There should be, if you like, stages, where at some amount of data the model has learned the local correlations but not the long-range ones. And in fact when you train transformers on these synthetic grammars, and also when you look at real language models, there is this signature. With little data the text is locally coherent and globally meaningless, and as you add data the coherence length grows. And that coherence length, we argue, is tied directly to how deep in the hierarchy the model has gotten.

The second connection is to diffusion models, where it becomes almost visible. In a diffusion model you add noise and then you denoise. And if the data is hierarchical, then what happens is that a small amount of noise changes low-level features, say a few characters or a few pixels, and the high-level latent, the meaning, is preserved. But there is a critical amount of noise at which the top of the hierarchy is suddenly lost, and the model can reconstruct a perfectly plausible sample that has a completely different global meaning. It is a kind of phase transition. And we see this in real image diffusion models and in language diffusion models too. So to me that is strong evidence that the hierarchical picture is not just a cartoon, it actually captures something that these models exploit.

So if you ask what it means for building better models, I would say the honest answer is that it gives you a theory of why they work at all, and what the right notion of difficulty is. Difficulty is not dimension, it is depth of the hierarchy and how much noise there is at each level. And then you can start to ask more precise questions. What architecture inductive biases let you climb the hierarchy faster. Whether you can detect the level a model has reached and target the data accordingly. Those are the things I find exciting, because we are moving from "deep learning works, it is mysterious" to something where you can actually make quantitative predictions and check them.

r001.rationale: The response confidently argues that hierarchical structure helps explain how models learn; it does not express uncertainty about whether fully understanding that hierarchy can be used efficiently for token-level prediction.

r002.rationale: The response describes latent variables and hierarchical generation, but does not distinguish understanding structure as an encoding problem from generating low-level data as a decoding problem.

astra-6.text:
I think the connection is that language has structure at many levels, and these levels are not independent. The choice of a word depends on the sentence, but the sentence also depends on the topic and on what you are trying to communicate. So, to predict well, a model has to infer something about these hidden variables from the text it observes.

The question is whether learning this structure requires an enormous number of examples, or whether the hierarchy itself makes learning more efficient. You can imagine learning simple features and then reusing them to understand more complex relationships. But you can also imagine that some relationships only become visible once you have enough data to connect different levels.

I find simplified models useful here. If we construct a distribution with a known hierarchy, we can ask precisely what a neural network learns, how much data it needs, and whether it generalizes to combinations it has never seen. That gives us a way to investigate mechanisms that are difficult to isolate in a large language model.

Of course, showing that something works in a simplified setting does not immediately give you a better language model. But it can tell you what matters: which statistical dependencies must be learned, where the difficulty lies, and whether an architecture is using the available structure efficiently. For me, that is the connection between understanding the hierarchy and improving generation.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty about how much data is needed to learn hierarchical structure, but does not express uncertainty about whether complete understanding of that hierarchy can be used efficiently for token-level prediction.

r002.rationale: The response does not distinguish understanding the world's structure as an encoding problem from generating low-level data as a decoding problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two questions here. One is whether language has a hierarchical structure, and the other is whether understanding that structure helps us explain how a model learns. You can generate convincing text without having an explicit theory of either, but a theory might tell us why some dependencies are learned easily and others require enormous amounts of data.

Imagine a simple generative process where high-level choices constrain lower-level choices, which eventually produce the words you observe. The learning problem is to infer those hidden relationships from the words alone. Then you can ask quite precise questions: How many examples do you need to discover a feature at a particular level? Can you reuse what you have learned in a new combination? What determines whether you generalize or simply memorize?

The useful thing about such a model is that you know the underlying structure, so you can measure whether the network actually discovers it. Of course, real language is much more complicated than a tree. The point is to isolate a mechanism. If we understand what controls learning in that setting, we may be able to make better decisions about architectures and data, rather than relying entirely on increasing scale.

r002.rationale: It describes inferring hidden relationships from observed words and generating words from high-level choices, but does not distinguish understanding structure as an encoding problem from low-level generation as a decoding problem.
